config.title: Optimistic UI

intro.title: Optimistic UI
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple like counter for a social media post that updates instantly when clicked, providing immediate feedback to the user. You'll learn the core concept of Optimistic UI, where the interface is updated optimistically before the server confirms the action, making the app feel faster and more responsive. The main technologies involved are React for building the component, TypeScript for type safety, and the useState hook to manage the like count state. By the end, you'll understand how to implement this pattern to enhance user experience in your applications.
intro.usecase: Optimistic UI is a crucial pattern for creating responsive interfaces in modern web applications. You'll see this implemented in social media platforms when users like or comment on posts, where the UI updates immediately while the request processes in the background. E-commerce sites use it extensively for shopping cart interactions, allowing users to add or remove items without waiting for server confirmation. This pattern is also essential in collaborative tools like document editors and project management dashboards, where multiple users need to see real-time updates to maintain workflow efficiency.

objectives: Initialize a state variable to manage the optimistic UI data.
Implement a handler function to update the optimistic state before an API call.
Apply a conditional rendering pattern to display the optimistic UI.
Integrate an asynchronous function to perform the actual data mutation.
Configure error handling to revert the optimistic state on API failure.
Manipulate the UI to reflect loading states during the optimistic update.

steps.title: Define the data interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named Task with three properties: id (number), title (string), and completed (boolean).
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions with their types.
steps.expectedOutcome: A Task interface is defined with the correct property types.
successCriteria: The Task interface is defined with id: number, title: string, and completed: boolean properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure all three properties (id, title, completed) are included with the correct types.

steps.hint: Use useState<Task[]> with an array of task objects matching your Task interface as the initial value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The tasks state is initialized with an array of Task objects, ready for optimistic updates.
successCriteria: tasks state is declared with useState
initial value is an array with at least one task object
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure tasks is typed as Task[] and has initial sample data.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've declared tasks state with useState, typed it as Task[], and provided initial sample data.

steps.title: Define the toggle handler function
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a function named handleToggle that takes a task id parameter and toggles the completed status of the matching task in the tasks state.
steps.hint: You'll need to use setTasks to update the state. Map over the tasks array and toggle completed for the task with the matching id.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleToggle function is defined that will toggle the completed status of a task when called with its id.
successCriteria: The handleToggle function is defined with a task id parameter and updates the tasks state using setTasks.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your handleToggle function takes an id parameter and properly toggles the completed status using setTasks.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleToggle function isn't quite right. It should take a task id parameter and update the tasks state by toggling the completed property of the matching task.

steps.title: Update the toggle handler for optimistic UI
steps.instruction: Inside the handleToggle function, first update the tasks state optimistically by toggling the completed status of the task with the given id,
steps.hint: Use setTasks to update the state immediately with the new completed value. Then use setTimeout to simulate a delay and revert the change if needed.
steps.expectedOutcome: The handleToggle function will immediately update the UI when called, then simulate an API call that may revert the change on failure.
successCriteria: handleToggle updates tasks state optimistically before setTimeout, and includes a setTimeout that may revert the change.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you update the state optimistically first, then add the setTimeout to simulate the async operation.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleToggle function should first update the state optimistically, then simulate an async API call with setTimeout.

steps.title: Add error handling to the toggle handler
steps.instruction: Inside the handleToggle function, add a try-catch block to wrap the optimistic update and simulated API call. In the catch block, revert the state update using setTasks with the previous tasks.
steps.hint: Use try { ... } catch { ... } to handle errors. Inside the catch block, call setTasks with the previous tasks array to rollback the optimistic update.
steps.expectedOutcome: The handleToggle function should include a try-catch block that catches errors and reverts the optimistic update by restoring the previous tasks array.
successCriteria: The handleToggle function contains a try-catch block with setTasks called in the catch block to revert the state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to include both the try block for the optimistic update and the catch block for reverting with setTasks.

steps.title: Map over tasks to display list items
steps.instruction: Inside the empty <ul> element, map over the tasks state to render an <li> element for each task. Each list item should display the task's title.
steps.hint: Use the map method on the tasks array. Inside the map callback, return an <li> with the task's title as content. Remember to add a unique key prop to each <li>.
steps.expectedOutcome: The task list will be displayed with each task's title in a bulleted list.
successCriteria: The <ul> contains a map over the tasks array that renders an <li> for each task, with each task's title displayed and a unique key prop assigned.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're mapping over the tasks array and returning an <li> with the task's title and a key prop.
steps.feedbackWrong: The list items aren't being rendered correctly. Check that you're using the map method on the tasks array and returning proper JSX elements.

steps.title: Add checkboxes and wire the toggle handler
steps.instruction: Inside each list item, add a checkbox input element. Bind its checked attribute to task.completed and wire its onChange event to call handleToggle with the task's id.
steps.hint: Use the map function's task parameter to access each task's completed status and id. The onChange handler should be an arrow function that calls handleToggle(task.id).
steps.expectedOutcome: Each task in the list will display with a checkbox that reflects its completed status. Clicking the checkbox will trigger the handleToggle function with the corresponding task id.
successCriteria: Checkbox inputs are added inside list items with checked={task.completed} and onChange={() => handleToggle(task.id)} attributes.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added checkboxes, but make sure they're properly wired: checked should bind to task.completed and onChange should call handleToggle(task.id).
steps.feedbackWrong: The checkboxes aren't properly configured. Each checkbox needs checked={task.completed} and onChange={() => handleToggle(task.id)} inside the map function.
